# Postmortem on Two States in Caller Integration Testing

This record started out as just a note alongside the integration testing session, stating that the constructor differed from the old record and that the weak pointer was later able to recover. As the original record, recovery page, samples, and card actions were uncovered one after another, the page grew longer, but the initial gap did not disappear as a result: the current entry point reported different values for current revision at two points in time, and what happened in between has still not been reconstructed.

The focus throughout has been on real call samples involving plugin and extension. They fall within unreal · Client Integration's own adaptation boundary and have their own schedules, maintainers, and exit criteria. This document records an instance of inconsistent object state and its recovery process, without incorporating observations from adjacent projects into this timeline.

## The First Few Lines Recorded

The first time the entry point was compared, the constructor was found to differ from the old record. At that point, there was not enough information to describe a complete call sequence, and all that could be confirmed was that the text at the current entry point differed from the old record. The early notes quickly summarized this as "two states of the same object", and this description was later retained because it accurately captured the confusion at the time, yet went further than the actual evidence.

What could be confirmed at the time was that there was a record from each of two points in time, not that exactly the same input had been used at both points. Screenshots without an account, version, and run id cannot fill in the request context for us; likewise, there is no material showing that only one change occurred between these two points in time. The initial description of "the same object" still needed to be checked and should not be taken to mean that object identity had already been confirmed.

The files from the session were stored in `docs/adj-unreal/incidents/unreal-client-integration-same-object-two-states.md` from the start. This was not a directory entry point created later just to organize the postmortem. The original record, recovery page, and unconfirmed causes were retained separately because they answer different questions: the original record shows that the initial deviation was observed, the recovery page shows that a particular user flow became usable again later, and the unconfirmed items show that an explanation of what happened between the two is still missing.

The first version left a field unfilled:

Missing point in time: ____

This empty field was not deleted. It was not a formatting omission, but a reflection of the fact that the original material had not preserved the actions between the two entry-point records along with their times. Later versions added a sequence table, but did not disguise relative order as wall-clock time.

## Why the Initial Response Stopped at Preserving the Evidence

After the initial deviation, the most immediate impulse was to keep triggering the same call to try to observe the difference again. This attempt was not pursued further. Repeated triggering would produce new observations, but would not recover the actions already missing from the earlier window; if a new round produced only green results, it would instead be easy to misplace those new results in the context of the initial deviation.

Therefore, the entry-point version was saved at the time, and the old screenshots were also retained. The later recovery result was not allowed to overwrite the original input. This action may seem conservative, but it prevented a very specific misreading: describing "currently usable" as "there was no anomaly at the time". The recovery page can only show what was seen after recovery, and cannot rewrite the fact that the initial deviation had already occurred.

The earliest materials were very terse, even making "stop further retries" sound like a conclusion. The actual meaning was narrower: without complete input and intermediate records, new run results would no longer be used to fill in the story of the original session. If a new state appears later, it should be appended as a new observation, rather than used to patch up the old screenshots.

Samples of plugin and extension were not split into larger runtime issues at this step either. They were simply adaptation targets being checked during caller-side integration testing. There was no evidence that the names, statuses, or remediation actions of other projects matched the changes here, so attribution was not extended to adjacent projects at the time.

## Recoverable relative order

Later, someone reordered the scattered observations by relative position. The table does not show exact times, nor is it a system-generated event sequence; it merely helps preserve "what was seen first and what was seen later."

| Relative position | Observations left in the original record | Subsequent handling | What this step does not indicate |
|---|---|---|---|
| T+00 | `unreal-caller-side integration-same object appears in two states` First deviation from the old baseline; constructor did not match the old record | Preserve the original input and entry-point version | Does not indicate that the input was exactly the same, nor that the cause of the deviation was found |
| T+07 | stream was still normal | Narrow the checks to the object where the difference appeared | Does not indicate that the entire call path was normal |
| T+18 | The comparison result was near bridge | Continue checking along the entry point | Does not indicate that bridge was the responsible object or the point where the change occurred |
| T+31 | User path was restored | Record the recovery result separately | Does not indicate that the two states have been fully explained |

T+00 is the starting point of this record. The difference between it and the old baseline is the observed constructor result, not a complete explanation of the object lifecycle, entry-point generation, or caller version. The old baseline can be used for comparison, but it did not preserve all the inputs needed to reconstruct the intervening process.

T+07 once led to a very tempting conclusion: since stream was normal, the issue should not be here. On later review, that statement was retracted. A normal stream only means that this local observation did not simultaneously show an anomaly; it cannot support the inference that the object state before, after, or in a parallel position to stream remained unchanged.

The bridge at T+18 should be understood the same way. The comparison pointing attention to the area around bridge is a localization signal, not an attribution. Early records phrased it too much like "the location had been found"; subsequent review reduced that conclusion back to a comparison result. Without complete logs and a reproduction using the same input, it is not possible to infer from "appeared nearby" that it was "caused by this."

After T+31, the user path became available again. This is the change that actually occurred in the incident and must be retained; however, there is no reason to merge the recovery time with the root-cause confirmation time. The original failure window still needs to be preserved; otherwise, people later will see only a green page and will not know that a different current revision had appeared before recovery.

## What that state diagram left behind

A very small state diagram was drawn in the second version to make handoff easier. It did not describe the system's internal states, nor did it attempt to map out the full call relationships involving plugin and extension. The nodes in the diagram only record how the materials were handled.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Seen: State deviation received
    Seen --> Compared: Compare entry point and old records
    Compared --> Restored: User path restored
    Compared --> Open: Cause still unknown
    Open --> Compared: New incident evidence arrives
```

`Seen` indicates that the initial deviation was saved; it does not mean that the same object had already been pinned down at the time of discovery. `Compared` indicates that the entry point and old records were examined together; it does not mean that the comparison covered all variables. `Restored` only indicates that the user path was restored, while `Open` preserves the state in which the cause and intermediate actions remain unknown.

The diagram has separate transitions from `Compared` to `Restored` and `Open` to avoid treating recovery as the endpoint of an explanation. Both things were indeed true in the incident: the user path later became usable, while it was still unknown why the observations from the two entry points differed. The diagram does not provide a hidden fifth node to stand in for the missing logs, because no such node exists in the materials.

If a similar phenomenon occurs again later, this diagram cannot be used directly as a handling script either. It can only remind whoever takes over not to skip the original records: first confirm whether they are seeing the same entry point, the same object, and the same type of call sample, then decide whether the new observation should be linked to the previous window or retained as a separate incident record.

## Differences Between Screenshots, Samples, and Logs

The materials handed over earlier consisted mainly of a screenshot and an old link. A screenshot can show that a particular row of results was seen, but it cannot reconstruct the full request context. Without an account, version, or run id, readers cannot know why another path was still working normally, nor can they determine whether the two entry-point observations were made under the same calling conditions.

This gap once led to a premature judgment. Someone initially relied on memory to explain the phenomenon as an entry-point switch, but follow-up questions about the specific input revealed that the screenshot had not included the input. As a result, "entry-point switching" was not written into the current conclusion. It can still be retained in the earlier paragraph as a working hypothesis raised at the time, but it cannot be treated as the sole cause.

A sample was attached later. The sample meant that the materials were no longer limited to a screenshot and could also help locate the dual-state sample again; it did not become a substitute for the missing logs. The observations covered by the sample and those covered by the old screenshot were not the same, and the two cannot be pieced together into a complete request just because they both point to the same event.

Another log segment was not retrieved at the time. This was because last night's job had already expired, and the logs could not be fetched for the time being. This fact is very specific and also places strict limits on the conclusions: the missing logs mean that actions between the two current revision values cannot be added to the timeline based on speculation. Even if a successful run occurs later, its output cannot be used to replace the expired log segment.

The original screenshot, samples, entry-point version, and recovery page therefore continued to be kept side by side. They are related, but they are not copies that can replace one another. Preserving this untidiness is closer to the actual situation than organizing everything into a smooth narrative: different materials answered questions at different levels at different times.

## Revisions to the Initial Explanations

The first early explanation was "the old link pointed to the wrong entry point". It came from a comparison recalled from memory, rather than a complete request. After it was later confirmed that the current entry point returned different current revision values at two points in time, this explanation was insufficient to account for all the observations: even if the old link did have a problem, that alone could not explain where the difference between the two points in time came from. It was therefore no longer retained as the sole cause.

The second explanation was "stream is normal, so bridge can be ruled out". This assessment is no longer valid either. The normal stream at T+07 was only a local observation, while the comparison at T+18 still lay near bridge. The two records do not cancel each other out; they only show that different locations did not exhibit the same phenomenon.

The third explanation was "the weak pointer is restored, so the state is already consistent". The recovery action did make the user path usable again, but the constructor differences were not compared again using the same input. Equating successful recovery with state consistency would overextend the significance of the recovery page.

None of these revisions produced a new overarching cause. Their purpose is to remove unsupported inferences: the old link cannot be used to explain all the changes, a locally normal stream cannot be used to rule out bridge, and weak pointer recovery cannot be used to override the constructor differences. The remaining conclusions are narrower than the early one-liners, but they are also closer to the saved records.

## Why the Recovery Page Did Not Replace the Original Page

After recovery, the user path was usable again. This result needs to be explicitly recorded, because it affects whether the caller can continue working afterward; but it is not an instruction to delete the original failure window. The first deviation in the original record and the subsequent state on the recovery page correspond to different observation times.

If only the recovery page were saved, future readers would understand the situation as having always been usable, or mistakenly believe that there had never been two revision values. If only the original failure window were saved, the current state would be incorrectly recorded as still unable to proceed. The purpose of keeping both pages is not to create a contradiction, but to let each point in time retain its own context.

The fact that the weak pointer can be restored must be recorded only on the recovery side. It shows that the recovery action produced a result in that observation, not that all related state returned to what was in the old record, nor that the cause of the changes in Unreal has been confirmed. This boundary was mentioned in the first version and was not expanded later just because the postmortem grew longer.

After recovery, the issue was not then passed off to unity or other peripheral projects. The call samples, adaptation boundaries, maintainer, and exit criteria for unreal · Client Integration remained within this project. The status of neighboring projects may be worth checking separately, but it is not material for this postmortem to use in filling the gap between the two entry-point records.

## The cards provide navigation, not a root-cause table

During subsequent organization, PRTA-006, PRTA-012 and PRTA-019 were all linked to this material. They each have a specific purpose and cannot be collapsed into a single "incident progression" record.

PRTA-006 corresponds to preserving the recovery results alongside the original incident context. The related work also included one instance of blocked log retrieval: last night's job had already expired, and the logs could not be pulled for the time being. This information explains why a section of the record could not be filled in; it does not explain why the object's state changed.

PRTA-012 is used to find the entry point for checking the dual-state samples. After the samples were attached, it was easier to review the incident context than with screenshots alone, but the samples were not complete logs and did not turn the window between the two revisions into a replayable process. They are useful for helping confirm that a particular sample exists, not for replacing the missing input.

PRTA-019 is associated with the "two record versions with the intervening records missing" thread. Later, the toolchain was pinned and the person taking over changed, indicating that work on the material continued. Toolchain pinning and the handoff are not proof of a state change, nor can they automatically connect T+00 and T+31.

An even later note pointed out that an expiration action had been sent to the wrong card and did not belong to the same incident context as "two record versions with the intervening records missing". This correction does only one thing: it removes that similar action from the inferences about this incident. It did not recover the logs, did not prove which revision produced the deviation, and did not change the still-unconfirmed relationship between bridge and constructor.

Cards therefore serve only a navigational purpose. When comparing the recovery result side by side with the original incident context, check PRTA-006; when checking the dual-state sample, check PRTA-012; when checking the trail where the intermediate record is missing, check PRTA-019. The order of card actions cannot replace the original observations in the entry file, especially not by putting a card action that was later corrected back into the timeline.

## A revised understanding of "the same object"

The "dual-state" in the page title can easily lead one to assume first that the object's identity has already been established. Initially, the evidence was not that strong. What can be compared is the corresponding wording in the entry record and the old record; the constructor differs, and the two time points show different current revision values. None of this is sufficient on its own to prove that the two observations share the same request context.

Therefore, when "the same object" is used now, it means the object clues placed together for cross-checking in this integration session, not an automatically established assertion of runtime identity. It is still necessary to check whether the entry, current observation, and invocation sample can be accounted for side by side. The fact that the names match, or that both pieces of material mention plugin and extension, is not enough to merge them directly.

This adjustment also explains why the old paragraph was not completely rewritten. The early incident context did indeed refer to it as two states of the same object; later, it was discovered that this wording included confirmation that had not yet been completed, so it was left in the language used at the time while its limitations were explained later. This lets readers see how the judgment was narrowed, rather than mistakenly believing that the complete facts were known from the outset.

## Current review sequence

When taking this issue over again, first open `docs/adj-unreal/incidents/unreal-client-integration-same-object-two-states.md`; do not start with the last line of green output. The original record contains the first deviation, while the recovery page contains the subsequent recovery; both need to be viewed together.

Next, verify whether the current revision for each of the two time points is still separately visible. If only a screenshot is available, first record the missing account, version, and run id as gaps; do not turn a line of results in the screenshot into a complete request. If the entry record can no longer be compared, retain that fact rather than reconstructing the same input from memory.

When two states appear again in a new incident context, first ask three local questions: Is it still the same entry point, can it be matched to the same object clue in the old record, and is it a sample from the same type of plugin or extension invocation? If any one of the three questions cannot currently be answered, save the new observation separately rather than forcing it back into T+00.

Even when the user path remains usable, keep the original anomaly window as well. The green result only indicates that the path recovered on that occasion; it does not automatically write back to the old incident context. The recovery result for weak pointer can be labeled a recovery observation, but it cannot be used to answer why Unreal changed.

When the comparison point lands near bridge again, record where it appears and the input at that time. Do not directly translate "nearby" as "cause". If the log is still expired, state that the log is missing; the next successful run will not serve as a substitute for the intervening window. If the card actions look similar, first verify the card objects; do not reassign to this incident an expiry action that has already been confirmed to have been sent to the wrong card.

## Keep the impact scope limited to the caller's context

The affected set is this group of real call samples in unreal · Client Integration. Before recovery, the two observations at the current entry point could not be directly combined into one stable record; after recovery, the user path became usable again, but that did not make the old observations invalid.

The impact description does not extend to projects without a shared context. plugin and extension are object terms associated with the call samples here, not a basis for automatically grouping all projects that use these terms into the same incident. Other projects may have their own maintenance records, their own recovery processes, and their own exit conditions; they are not included in this postmortem's causal assessment.

This is also why this page has not put unrelated cards in the timeline. The postmortem is organized only around the local information in the original records, recovery page, samples, and three related cards that have already been saved. If gaps still remain between the materials, leave those gaps here.

## Incomplete items

- The specific actions that occurred between the two current revision entries have still not been reconstructed.
- Whether the input changed between T+00 and T+07 is not recorded.
- There is no material showing whether the bridge comparison point at T+18 was related to the difference from constructor.
- There is no new reproduction record showing whether the dual state could still be reproduced with the same input after weak pointer recovery.
- It has not been confirmed whether the expired job's logs were retained elsewhere.
- The account, version, and run id missing from the original screenshot have not yet been filled in from the existing materials.

These items are not abstract risks listed to make the incident write-up sound cautious. Each corresponds to a concrete gap that had already appeared in the incident context: there are two entry records, with the action between them missing; the screenshot has a result but lacks request context; the recovery page has a green result but lacks a re-comparison under the same input; an attempt was made to retrieve the logs, but the job had already expired at that time.

If additional material is found later, it should be appended after the existing records, with a note identifying which window it fills. Do not rewrite the original observation at T+00 just to make the timeline complete, and do not replace the expired log with a new successful run. If an early assessment is subsequently shown to be inaccurate, retain the old wording and the order in which it was corrected.

## Retain the old paragraphs

The following sentences come from the early records; they are retained to show what could be seen at the time; they do not by themselves constitute the current conclusion.

> constructor is different from the old record.
>
> weak pointer can be recovered, but it is still unknown why Unreal changes.
>
> Keep the original entry point for now; do not retry.

The first sentence refers to the observation of the initial deviation, not an identification of the root cause. The second sentence only indicates that the recovery action produced a result and the cause remains unknown, not that the constructor difference has disappeared. The third sentence describes the approach used at the time to prevent new observations from overwriting the earlier window, not a fixed procedure applicable to all future integration testing.

An earlier paraphrase also said "stream is normal, so bridge can be ruled out". That passage no longer applies. The records at T+07 and T+18 are both still retained: the former shows normal behavior in part of stream, and the latter is a comparison point near bridge. Together, they qualify the earlier paraphrase, but do not provide a new, complete causal attribution.

The page's progression from empty entries in the first version, to relative times and a state diagram in the second version, and then to the samples, expired logs and corrections to erroneous cards added this time, reflects how the materials gradually became available. The recovery result came after the initial deviation, and the card corrections came after the samples were organized; these layers should not be sanitized into an incident account that appears to have been complete from the start.

For now, this page is still maintained within the scope of unreal · Client Integration's on-site context. Recovery of the user path is a recorded outcome; there are still gaps in the intermediate actions, confirmation of object identity and assessment of the cause. Further additions will be made only when new entry-point records, samples or usable logs become available.

# Caller Integration Testing Exit Procedure

When triggered, check only three things: the exit action, the last visible result, and whether the adj-unreal side has already exited. Release success is not determined here; the relevant owner must sign off on that separately.

1. Open `docs/adj-unreal/release/unreal-client-integration-exit-window-checklist.md` and first record the `metadata` you saw before the window started. If that record is missing, don't create a new one from memory.
2. After the exit action is issued, retain the last result you saw, then clean up. If you see `FName`, don't clean up yet; at the time, it was only a marker for continued monitoring, not a success signal.
3. If `MCP` hasn't appeared, stop here. Don't run additional paths just to close the window, and don't mark anything that hasn't appeared as complete.

If any temporary routing or permissions are still in place, remove them first; if the queue keeps accepting new work after they're removed, the window is not over: restore the original entry point and retain the result from that point.

TODO: The restore action hasn't been tried in the shared environment yet. Next time, add at least a snippet of the last result after an actual restore; release decisions not listed here still need confirmation from the original owner.

# Caller Integration Exit Procedure

This page is still maintained in the form originally used for the window: it only checks the exit action, the last visible result, and the exit action on the adj-unreal side. It is not a release sign-off sheet. Whether release is allowed after the window ends is still up to the corresponding owner; the checklist only gives the person taking over a sequence that avoids clearing the environment too early.

The entry is still at `docs/adj-unreal/release/unreal-client-integration-exit-window-checklist.md`. This path is where the materials currently available for review are kept, and the body and attachments are maintained by unreal · Client Integration. Before the window starts, record side by side the checklist version in use, the current revision, and the first visible result; when the entry changes, do not directly subtract the statistics from before and after the entry change.

## What to Leave When Opening the Window

- [ ] Keep the record corresponding to the original input. If only a screenshot remains, do not treat it as a basis for reconstructing the original request.
- [ ] Record the last visible result before exit, together with the entry used at the time; a later green result cannot overwrite this record.
- [ ] Check whether any routes still point to the old exit action. Save a snapshot of the route before the change before deleting it.
- [ ] Document the temporary permissions or bypasses actually used this time, and mark where they are to be removed. The project's release decision is not recorded here.

The first version treated `FName` as a "don't clear the environment yet" prompt and treated the absence of `MCP` as a stopping point. These two terms remain in the old checklist because the window was closed on that basis at the time; they cannot by themselves prove that the current access path has exited. When taking over, first check this run's input and the last result, then determine whether those two old prompts are still relevant.

## Exit Actions

1. After issuing the exit action agreed for this window, do not immediately clear the routes, screenshots, or input records. First confirm that the adj-unreal side is not still using the old entry.
2. If the old route is still present, first retain a snapshot from before the change, then remove the pointer to that action. If new work still enters after deletion, stop the window-closing process and restore the original route; do not rewrite other integration logic in the same window.
3. Revoke the temporary permissions and bypasses opened for this window. If the queue still accepts new work after revocation, treat it as not exited, restore the entry just removed, and record the last result.
4. After exit, record the last visible result. It may be a state still in flight or a state that has already stopped; do not just extract a log line that looks like "success".

Here, "last" means the actual result most recently visible before closing the window, not a conclusion assembled afterward. If the entry has changed, just note the time of the change alongside it. Keep data from the old entry as-is and observe the new entry separately, to avoid combining numbers from different conditions into a trend.

## Stopping and Rollback

If any of the following occurs, stop this round; do not continue trying to complete the result with substitute input:

- The original request is missing; only a screenshot remains;
- Work still enters through the old route after exit;
- A temporary permission or bypass cannot be removed, or the queue continues to accept new work after removal;
- Determining the result requires going beyond the current interface of adj-unreal.

After stopping, first roll back the routes or entries just changed in this round, while retaining the original input, the pre-change snapshot, and the last visible result. Whether the restoration actually took effect must be checked once more in the environment used at the time; any recovery action that has not been exercised remains marked not exercised, and speculation must not replace the result.

PRTA-018 is a navigation card for the rollback entry point and stop conditions. If the scenario on the card has not actually been exercised, leave it marked not exercised in the checklist; do not write "rollback completed" just because "a rollback entry point exists".

## Handoff

When the window cannot be reproduced because of the core module's release window, stop at the existing materials; do not recreate a similar input. PRTA-004 has screenshots, but the original request is not attached; this card can only help locate "the replay of the original input unreal-client-integration", not provide new replay material.

The current handoff owner continues to follow up on the action for the current revision; do not rewrite records from the old shift. PRTA-017 is used to locate this entry; it does not change the last result retained in the previous window. PRTA-005 records the route remnants of the old exit action, and PRTA-011 records that the trend before and after the entry change cannot be compared directly. The related cards are used only for navigation here; they do not replace the window-closing actions in this checklist.

The last item is still a manual check: confirm that adj-unreal has carried out this exit action, and write any incomplete items next to the original record. If only permission revocation or route deletion was completed and the last visible result was not retained, the window is still considered not closed.

# Caller Integration Entry Point Migration Guide

In integration testing, a batch of plugin and extension call samples still comes through the old entry point. Having new names in the directory too doesn't mean callers have switched; use the actual consumers' integration results to determine whether migration is complete. The index file is at `docs/adj-unreal/migration/current-entry-old-entry-migration-index.md`; it retains the old entry points, replacement locations, and callers still using the old entry points.

The two paths being compared are:

| Original path | Current handling | What to check first during migration |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `weak pointer` | Integrate through the entry point split out for Unreal | Which failure exit the call sample reaches |
| Compatibility calls in the old entry point | The current entry point retains the corresponding adaptation point | Whether the caller still actually loads the plugin or extension |

The initial idea was to continue along `weak pointer`, but the index later showed that the two sections had different failure exits. With Unreal split out, integration feedback can be filed by call sample, without having to mix the two exits in a single migration. Here, "current entry point" refers only to this integration-testing path; this says nothing about identically named entry points in other projects.

## Switchover order

1. First, find a caller in the index that is still using the old entry point, and confirm whether its integration sample is for a plugin or an extension.
2. Cross-check the old entry point and its replacement location, then switch that caller to the separate Unreal entry point; move only one sample at a time.
3. Record the exit actually reached at the adaptation point. If both the new and old paths are reachable but the exits differ, stop at that sample and do not count it as migrated.
4. Repeat the integration with the actual consumer. Only remove the old call from the "still in use" column once the integration feedback is stable.
5. Keep the migration records and exit criteria for this batch in one place so the directory status does not get ahead of the callers' status.

`constructor` was once left alongside the index as a marker for a specific case; it only helps locate the call being examined at the time and does not indicate that all construction paths have been migrated. Assess `metadata` and `retainer` only from their respective sample records as well; do not include similarly named side paths in the same batch.

## Returning to the old entry point

If, after integrating through the new entry point, the caller cannot finish loading or the failure exit differs from the one on the sample's original path, first remove the new-entry-point integration for this sample, then restore the corresponding old entry point listed in the index. After restoration, still go by that caller's actual usage results; do not mark recovery as complete just because the old directory still exists. Once the old entry point has been successfully restored, keep this sample in the "still in use" column for separate handling next time.

The callers currently using `PInvoke` have not yet been fully identified. Keep entries involving it on the old path and out of the switchover batch above. CI can record the post-migration integration point, but cannot replace confirmation from actual callers.

Leave any old notes that cannot be checked in place in the index, and mark them as outdated; do not use records from similar pages to fill in the details of this case.

# Compatibility Catalog: Proposal for an Approach Not Taken

This proposal remains in the catalog because the debate at the time did not simply go away: some wanted `IL2CPP` listed separately from the compatibility catalog, while others insisted on continuing to maintain a single entry point through `MCP`. The approach described here was ultimately not pursued, but deleting the proposal would make the catalog split look like just a naming change.

The initial premise was straightforward. `unity-compatibility-catalog` was dealing with both the old entry point and new compatibility entries. People reviewing the records often started with the catalog, then worked out which part they were dealing with. Those proposing the split believed that the two branches had different failure exits, and that keeping them together would cause issues to be grouped as the same type prematurely at the catalog level. Those opposed argued that the catalog's value was precisely in giving adopters a single place to look things up; once the branches were made public, subsequent maintenance effort would first go into explaining the differences between entry points.

The draft at the time laid out the proposal as the following two items, rather than as a commitment to implement it.

- Keep `MCP` as the original entry point to the compatibility catalog, and continue listing available entries under it.
- Create a separate catalog section for `IL2CPP` without replacing the old entry point initially; if a rollback is needed, prioritize restoring the original visible path.

Those supporting the second item saw it as a separation for troubleshooting, not an interface rework: first make it clear in the catalog which track readers had entered, then trace the differences separately. That sounded reasonable at the time and carried an implicit assumption—that callers could accept an additional stable fork in the catalog. That assumption was not confirmed.

The opposing view did not call for denying the differences in `IL2CPP`. The dispute was over where those differences should appear. If the differences were reflected in the catalog structure, the old entry point would still need to explain its relationship to the new section; if only one entry point was retained, maintainers would have to explain both cases within the entries. The first option put complexity in navigation; the second left it for readers to deal with each time. There was not enough material at the time to tell which cost was lower.

The draft also outlined a narrowly scoped trial: leave the old entry point unchanged, select only the `IL2CPP` entries that needed separate explanation, place them under the candidate section in a copy of the catalog, and observe whether adopters could still find them from the original location. This "observation" was not intended as a performance comparison or a presentation check; the only thing to check was whether the catalog directed people to the wrong compatibility notes. Since no set of adopters was defined in a way that could be recorded, this window never closed.

One old judgment needs to be preserved in particular: the two failure exits were different, so the catalog should be split. This was the proposal's central rationale at the time, but it did not become a confirmed catalog rule. In hindsight, that statement linked "different failure exits" too tightly to "the catalog must fork"; that does not, however, justify erasing the original concern. If the old entry point continues to serve as a rollback path, the catalog may still need an explicit note telling readers not to conflate the two sets of material.

The rollback conditions were only roughly defined at the time: if the old entry point cannot be restored after the split, or if adopters need to keep checking back and forth between two catalog locations, stop the trial and restore the single-track approach. "Restore" here referred only to the catalog entry point and entry locations; it did not include any additional adjustments for `ABI` callers. The scope of `ABI`'s use had not been verified when this proposal was drafted, so no compatibility commitments should be inferred from this old proposal.

There was also an unresolved migration question. If the catalog retained the old entry point while adding a new section, should old links continue pointing to the original entries, or point instead to locations with the new explanation? The first approach made rollback easier; the second could reduce duplicated explanations. The draft did not choose either. The related entry-point migration records were later stored separately at DOC-40; this page does not use those records to retroactively supply a decision that had not been completed at the time.

What is preserved here, then, is an approach that was not adopted: separate `IL2CPP` from `MCP`'s compatibility catalog in exchange for clearer local distinctions, while accepting the cost of the old entry point and the new section coexisting. It lacked sufficient evidence from adopters and did not proceed to implementation. If a similar split is proposed again during catalog maintenance, the old links, actual adopters, and rollback scope should be reconfirmed, rather than treating the preference expressed on this page as the standing conclusion.

The original material remains at `docs/adj-unity/proposals/not-adopted-unity-compatibility-catalog-route.md`. This file preserves the proposal and objections from that time, along with where things stopped.

flowchart LR

    I --> S{Observed behavior still within the normal sample range}
    S -- Yes --> K[Keep the existing path]
    S -- No --> O[Route to the relevant maintainer contact]
    O --> B[Continue reviewing only the bridge scope]

| Where the issue lands | First contact | What to include in the handoff | Not for this contact to answer |
|---|---|---|---|
| Project entry point | LICENSE · Dependency Boundary Audit duty contact | Entry point, time, first visible result | Long-term ownership of shared interfaces |
| `stream` behavior or artifacts | Module maintainer | Minimal symptoms visible to the user | Adoption decisions by actual users |
| `bridge` risks, licensing, or scope | Relevant decision-making contact | Original input and version | Specific implementation arrangements |

# Docs Site Entry Troubleshooting Tree

When the docs site entry point gets stuck, first confirm whether what you are looking at is the original failure state or a page from a rerun. The latter can show that it opens now, but it cannot replace the record of the former. Start with the entry point; do not infer the intermediate process from directory names, averages, or the final display. A page reached through an old link also cannot replace the state at the current entry point. If the two differ, record them separately.

```text
Is the original record available?
├─ No
│  └─ Return to the current entry point and fill in the original input, version, and first visible result; stop here
└─ Yes
   ├─ A recent known-good sample can be found
   │  ├─ The first difference is still within the docs site: check the entry point, resources, permissions, or index
   │  └─ The first difference appears outside an explicit interface: preserve the difference and hand it off to the maintainer of the current interface
   └─ No known-good sample
      └─ Record only where it stopped; do not name a root cause
```

The original record is the content left behind when the request entered the docs site at that time—not an edited screenshot or a green page from a later rerun. Keep the original input, version, and first visible result together so it is clear that the comparison target has not been quietly changed. If only the final display remains, first fill in the entry-side information; do not directly attribute a blank display page to the docs site implementation.

The version should be the version information corresponding to when the user entered the docs site, not a page the investigator selected later. The first result must also state whether the request was rejected, got stuck, or failed to progress further; do not leave only "failed." If the last state before failure can be confirmed, record it alongside the entry location. If it cannot be confirmed, leave it blank rather than filling it in with a guessed module name.

When a known-good sample is available, look only for the first difference between `stream` and the known-good sample. The before-and-after difference may be the state before and after entering the entry point, or content already displayed within the docs site; change only one condition at a time during comparison. Do not change the entry point and the version at the same time and then attribute the result to one or the other. If the first difference does not cross the docs site boundary, continue checking the docs site's own entry point, resources, permissions, or index. Do not skip a difference that is already visible just because the flow will later pass through `bridge`.

Having no known-good sample does not mean the docs site has no problem; it only means a comparison cannot be made this time. Record where it stopped and the inputs already available. The next person taking over should first add a sample or an entry record. Do not use the fact that a directory still opens or a tutorial is still accessible as a substitute for a known-good sample at the current entry point; the directory, tutorial, and page the user entered are not the same place.

If the difference really stops at `bridge`, this page does not determine the meaning of the interface. Bring the original input, version, first result, and first difference to the maintainer of the current interface. If the contract visible to users needs to change, or changing the behavior requires crossing an explicit interface, stop here and open a separate review; the docs-site side should retain only the confirmed entry-point state.

Two actions often mislead troubleshooting. First, treating a green result after a rerun as recovery; it only shows that this run did not reproduce the issue. Second, seeing that a directory or tutorial is still accessible and assuming the current entry point is healthy; the entry point, directory, and final display are not the same place. In both cases, return to the original record instead of expanding the speculation.

Before handoff, check four things: where it stopped, the original input, the version used, and the first result. If the state before failure has been confirmed, attach that as well. If any one item is missing, the person taking over can only collect the missing data, not pick up the root-cause investigation. Problems within the docs site stay with the docs site; only problems that cross an explicit interface are handed off.

# Resource Site Entry-Point Troubleshooting Tree

If there is a stall, an access denial, or a page that does not progress at the resource site's current entry point, first preserve the evidence at that entry point. Here, "current entry point" means the step the user actually took to enter unreal-compat-documentation-portal, not alternative paths later found through old links, index pages, or screenshots. When handling the issue, first determine whether the records are sufficient, then decide whether it should stay with the resource site or be handed to the current module maintainer.

An earlier version put "run it again and see" too early. After that retry, the page turned green, but the first failure sample was not saved; that lesson is retained here: retries may be used later for confirmation, but must not erase the original evidence first. Retain the input, version, and first stall location already obtained before the retry separately, and treat any later successful page only as a separate record.

```text
Entry point stalls or access is denied
│
├─ Can you provide the request/run id and the location of the denial or stall?
│  ├─ No
│  │  └─ Return to the current entry point to complete the record; do not discuss root causes without the first record
│  └─ Yes
│     ├─ Has the last verifiable state before the failure been added?
│     │  ├─ No: fill in this field, and stop the record here
│     │  └─ Yes
│     │     ├─ Is this a record left by the old exit entry point?
│     │     │  ├─ Yes: do not hand it off based on the old execution record; first check the current exit
│     │     │  └─ No: continue comparing the first difference
│     │     └─ Is there a recent known-good sample?
│        ├─ No: hand off only the entry-point evidence, without assigning a cause
│        └─ Yes
│           ├─ The first difference is still within the resource site's resources, permissions, or index
│           │  └─ Leave it with the resource site maintainers
│           └─ The first difference crosses a well-defined interface or stops at bridge
│              └─ Hand it to the current module maintainer; stop and enter review if the user-visible contract needs to change
```

## Preserve the entry-point evidence first

When access fails for a non-administrator, do not just write "there is a permissions issue". Record where the denial occurred and the `request/run id` for that attempt. The original card for PRTD-001 collects these two items: it asks for the denial location and the request/run id to be recorded back in the original location. If the person taking over receives an unnumbered secondhand account, a cleaned-up page, or a screenshot of a successful attempt, ask the other party to return to the current entry point and collect the missing evidence; without the first failure record, this page's procedure stops here.

Also add the last verifiable state before the failure. The task in PRTD-008 is precisely to fill in the preceding step from the current entry point, because knowing only that "the page did not progress" does not distinguish between an entry flow that has not yet reached the resource site and a step that has stalled within the resource site. Write this state as the location actually confirmed at the time, and do not fill the gap with a guessed module name. If it cannot be filled in, leave it blank and limit the handoff to the entry-point evidence.

Keep the original input, the version used, and the first visible result in the same record. Here, the version means the version information associated with the user's entry into the resource site on that attempt, not an explanatory page chosen later for troubleshooting. The first result must not be overwritten by a green result from a rerun, either. This at least lets the person taking over determine whether they are looking at the same type of entry point, rather than two pages that look identical but are actually different.

If the entry-point record comes from an old link, explicitly mark that the old link and the current entry point are not the same path. An old link can show what happened in the past, but cannot prove that the entry point the user is now going through has the same issue. The pre-failure state, denial location, and first result for the current entry point still need to be collected separately; without these, do not skip collection because there is a screenshot of the old page.

## Old exits and the former receiving team

The exit entry point has changed once, and execution records preserved from the previous incident did not cover the new exit. Therefore, when an old exit appears in a record, first confirm whether it is still the entry point the user is currently going through. If it is not, do not characterize the current entry point based on success or failure on the old path; keep the old record as a historical sample, then add the first record for the current exit.

Previously, the old routing sent execution records to a receiving team that had already been decommissioned. If you encounter such a handoff, do not keep chasing the former team, and do not reassign the issue to the resource site merely because no one in the former team responds. Hand it to the current module maintainer, and explain that the handoff is based on the current exit rather than the old execution record. The rationale in PRTD-002 for redirecting the handoff to the current module maintainer was likewise based on reviewing the existing implementation; this is more reliable than continuing to pass it along the old route.

Records from the old exit do not need to be deleted. They are still useful for determining "which version of the exit this execution record covers", but keep them separate from the entry-point record for this attempt when handing off. If the old record lacks a result for the current exit, it can only be attached to the ticket as background, and the person taking over must not be required to continue processing it through the former team or the old exit.

If the first difference in the entry point, resources, permissions, or index is still within the resource site, the resource site maintainers take over. At this point, attaching the entry-point location and first difference is enough, and there is no need to hand over subsequent speculation as well. For example, if the location where the user is denied access is clearly at the resource site's entry point, address that entry point's permission conditions first; do not switch to pursuing other pages just because there are nearby tutorials, indexes, or historical links.

## When samples are available, look only at the first change

If there is a recent known-good sample, compare the earliest point of disagreement in `stream`. Change only one condition per comparison: do not change both the entry point and the version, then attribute the result to either side. If the earliest difference is within the resource site, the resource site maintainers continue handling it; if the earliest difference is a stall at `bridge`, record that location, then hand it to the current module maintainer.

Before comparing, first confirm that the known-good sample really comes from a comparable entry point. If all you have is an index page, a tutorial page, or a page that was successfully opened later, do not treat them as known-good controls. Retain the original input and version used for the comparison, so that an entry-point change is not mistakenly recorded as a change within the resource site. If the first difference has not yet been located, record only the last confirmed state and do not yet categorize it as resources, permissions, or index.

`bridge` is not an automatic root-cause label. It is only the boundary for this page: troubleshooting has moved beyond what the resource site can confirm, and proceeding requires materials from the interface side. Include the original input, version, first result, and first difference in the handoff; if any of these is missing, the person taking over must complete the record first and should not directly change user-visible behavior.

If it is determined that the user-visible contract needs to change, or that behavior must be changed across a well-defined interface, this page's procedure stops at the handoff and enters formal review. The resource site maintainers can describe the entry-point evidence, but cannot make decisions on behalf of the interface side. Conversely, the interface side should not infer from the final displayed page that the resource site's entry point is already working correctly.

## When the on-call person is unavailable

When the on-call person for the resource site's core module is unavailable, entry-point records can still be supplemented, but interface assessment must not be delegated to the former receiving team. PRTD-008 was previously blocked by this situation; the existing request/run id, pre-failure state, and current exit should have been retained at that time, rather than redirecting it to a defunct former team just to keep the record moving.

While waiting for the current module maintainer, do not repeatedly run the same entry point to generate more records. If a rerun is genuinely needed, explicitly label it as a follow-up confirmation and keep it separate from the first failure sample. If the first sample is missing, the rerun result can only count as new evidence, and cannot be used to supply a conclusion about the original incident.

The on-call person's absence does not change the branch point. Entry-point, resource, permission, or index issues already confirmed within the resource site remain in the resource site's records; differences that have crossed a well-defined interface still go to the current module maintainer. Fields may be filled in and existing records organized during the absence, but this must not be used to reframe an interface assessment as a resource site conclusion.

## Review by someone other than the author

PRTD-002 requires someone who did not participate in the change to go through the original steps, using the original author's result only as a reference. The reviewer should first look at the original entry point, original input, and original version, then enter independently; they should not first be given a judgment about "what they should see". If the review does not reproduce the issue, still preserve the original evidence, and do not merge the two results into a single success.

If the first difference the reviewer sees is still within the resource site's scope, report it to the resource site maintainers; if it crosses a well-defined interface, hand it off through the current module maintainer's entry point. The purpose of the review is to confirm whether the branch point is reproducible, not to replace analysis by the interface side. The reviewer only needs to report the node they reached and the first result they preserved; do not add root causes for branches with no records.

## Records after a reply

After receiving confirmation from Unreal lazy-load compatibility · User Documentation Portal, update only the corresponding field, and leave adj-unreal-compat in its original state. PRTD-009 is for this kind of single-item update: confirmation of one item does not mean the old exit, other entry points, or unreviewed samples have also been corrected.

After receiving confirmation, first check which entry point, which record, and which field it applies to. If the reply confirms only one item within the resource site, retain the original states of the old exit and the interface-side branch; do not take a single confirmation to mean that the entire chain has recovered. If the confirmation concerns the current module maintainer's part, attach the original entry-point record to the reply as well, so that the new response is not sent to the former receiving team again.

When you need to revisit the existing entry-point instructions, use `docs/adj-unreal-compat/runbooks/unreal-compat-documentation-portal-stuck-who-to-escalate-to.md`. The related evidence cards are kept at PRTD-001, PRTD-002, PRTD-008 and PRTD-009; this page is only responsible for passing the location of the stall to the right recipient.

# nightly verifier decision record

This record captures how a nightly verifier review was brought to a close; it is not a generalized description of Tencent Runtime Systems. Two directions were on the table that could easily be described as the same thing: continue retaining the current mcp-transport entry, or continue moving forward around the adjustment window. Their subjects are adjacent, but their meanings differ. The former concerns whether the existing entry can still be called and reverted; the latter concerns which portion of the observed runtime behavior this round is willing to include in the approved scope.

The draft stated this distinction too briefly, making it read like "leave the old entry in place while starting the replacement." The review corrected that: this round did not approve unconditional replacement, nor did it treat the adjustment window as a completed global switch. What was approved was an evidence-constrained review scope; the old entry was explicitly left in place as a revertible retained item. This distinction determines what must be recorded during subsequent coordination, and it also means that objections cannot be deleted as if they were resolved issues.

## What was decided this time

1. The current mcp-transport entry will remain in place. This is not a verbal holding statement meaning "do not touch it for now," but the old entry to which this round's adjustment can return if it deviates.
2. The adjustment window may continue, but only the portion covered by existing materials is approved. The scope is determined by runtime boundaries that can actually be verified, and must not be extrapolated from names, guessed call relationships, or convenient implementation habits.
3. The integration lead will take responsibility for coordination. The coordination record must clearly state this round's actual impact, how far the window extends, and how the old entry will be retained when reverting; the core implementation side will add materials related to the entry and runtime boundaries.
4. Portions not covered by the materials remain open reservations. They are neither blockers nor default approval; if they are to be included in the adjustment later, supporting evidence must be added separately before they are discussed again.

"Retention" has two different meanings here. Retaining the mcp-transport entry ensures that an existing path still has a fallback point after this review. Retaining an open reservation acknowledges that the review did not then contain enough information to state certain extended judgments as facts. The former is an operational old entry; the latter is a gap in judgment. Calling both of them "temporarily retained" would obscure the actual decision.

The adjustment window should not be written as an abstract time term either. In this record, it means the scope of boundaries that this review is willing to continue processing, not advance permission for all related behavior. If an issue can only be explained by saying that it "should run along the same path," it has not entered the approved portion of the window. This limitation does not deny that a larger adjustment may be possible later; it simply refuses to mix unverified portions into this conclusion.

## Judgment adopted by the review

The meeting materials required treating behavior as a chain of boundaries that can be identified at runtime, rather than jumping from one implementation location directly to the entire system. The sentence retained in the review was: Treat behavior as a chain of observable runtime boundaries, and let repository evidence outrank convenient implementation folklore.

This sentence is not a slogan here. It is meant to restrain a specific tendency: seeing an existing entry, a call name, or packaged runtime code and rushing to treat them as a complete behavior graph. `unity/upms/webgl/Javascripts~/PuertsDLLMock/dist/puerts-runtime.js` was the file checked while following the entry and call names at the time, showing that the discussion remained grounded in repository objects; but its location does not automatically become permanent ownership, nor can that one location alone establish that the adjustment window covers all related boundaries.

Accordingly, the priority of this round's materials is clear. First examine repository evidence that can be mapped to runtime boundaries, then determine whether the window is broad enough; do not first assume that the window is sufficient and then select fragments that make the implementation appear smooth. This order also explains why the decision did not describe the "adjustment window" as a one-time completed modification: what could be confirmed at the time was the review boundary, not an implementation result that could be extended arbitrarily.

In this record, actual impact is documented by decision object rather than as an unverified expansion narrative: subsequent nightly verifier checks will address both the existing mcp-transport entry and the materials within the window; the integration side must retain the coordination entry; and the old entry must not lose its reversion significance merely because work within the window continues. Implementation replacements, caller scope, or broader runtime changes for which there is no evidence have not been recorded as impacts that occurred in this round.

## Approaches compared

**Retain only the current entry.** The advantage of this direction is that the fallback relationship is most direct, and the discussion does not first need to change the review scope. The objection is that it would misstate "the entry is still present" as "the current judgment is sufficient," causing the nightly verifier's review of materials within the window to remain stalled. The review did not adopt the claim that retaining the entry is equivalent to stopping the adjustment.

**Proceed directly according to the adjustment window.** This direction attempts to shift attention quickly to the processing scope represented by the window. The objection is also the most concentrated: if the runtime behavior at the edge of the window is not yet supported by materials, proceeding directly would make "under discussion" look like "already approved." It would also weaken the significance of the old entry, because if reversion later becomes necessary, the record would not clearly state which portion is being reverted and which portion is being retained.

**Retain the old entry and limit the window to the verified scope.** This is the combination adopted in this round. It is not a compromise that implements half of each proposal; it addresses two risks separately: the old entry provides the reversion path, while the evidence constraint prevents the approved scope from expanding. The coordinator must include both in subsequent records and must not report only one of "the window is open" or "the entry is unchanged."

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[Current mcp-transport entry] --> B[Retained as a revertible old entry]
    C[Adjustment window] --> D{Runtime boundaries covered by existing materials}
    D -- Yes --> E[Included in this round's approved scope]
    D -- No --> F[Open reservation, pending additional verification]
```

The two lines in the diagram deliberately do not converge into "replacement completed." Retaining the entry and approving the window each have their own conditions and different failure modes. If the judgment within the window later proves untenable, what is reverted is the approval within that scope, not the removal of the old entry as well; if the old entry itself needs adjustment, the existence of the window cannot be used to skip new verification.

## Revertible old entry

The old entry is required to remain not to permanently solidify the historical path. Its purpose is to give this decision a clear reverse action: if a subsequent review finds that the window's scope was expanded, that the boundaries were identified incorrectly, or that the materials cannot support the original approval, it must still be possible to return to the current mcp-transport entry. This means that reversion acts on an identifiable entry rather than on an unexecutable instruction to "restore the previous state."

Correspondingly, reversion does not mean rejecting all work within the window. What needs to be reverted is the judgment extending beyond the materials' coverage, along with the expectation of progress created by that judgment. Whether the portion supported by the materials should remain must be reassessed according to the boundaries that could be verified at the time. The draft did not distinguish these two layers, making it easy to assume that reversion meant choosing only between "retain everything" and "adjust everything"; this review rules out that misreading.

The conditions for reverting the old entry have not been compressed into a single signal. The current decision only requires the coordination record to identify which portion of the adjustment was approved, what kind of runtime verification that approval depends on, and which scopes become invalid when returning to the old entry. Pretending that an unverified boundary is a fixed threshold would recreate the extrapolation that this round deliberately avoided.

## What the coordination record should retain

The integration lead is not taking responsibility for redrawing implementation ownership, but for keeping this decision readable during subsequent verification. At a minimum, the record must place the actual impact, the window scope, and the reversion capability of the old entry within the same context. Actual impact should describe only object changes that have already occurred in the nightly verifier review: the existing entry was retained, the window was limited, and unverified items were not approved. Do not record possible subsequent call changes as results in advance.

When the core implementation side provides materials related to the entry, the focus is not on repeating the entire runtime implementation, but on enabling the review to determine whether a given boundary actually falls within the window. When the platform side participates in the review, it may object to whether the materials are sufficient to support the window judgment; its role is not to replace the integration side in declaring the scope, nor to turn the monitoring perspective into a new implementation commitment.

If the coordination process is left with only a conclusion that "the adjustment is complete," the record has lost the key conditions of this decision. Conversely, if it contains only the old entry without stating what was approved within the window, it cannot distinguish conservative retention from conditional progress. Both items should remain in the same coordination materials, but they must not be merged into one ambiguous state.

## Addendum to the draft

The value of the draft is that it promptly recorded two directions and several unresolved points, but its wording of "proceed according to the adjustment window" was too broad. After review, the historical position of this phrase is retained, while its meaning is narrowed to: proceed with the review only within the scope covered by existing materials; this does not mean that entry replacement has been completed, nor that behavior outside the entry is thereby approved.

Another point added was the coordinator. The earlier record only said that coordination was needed, without specifying its content; it now clearly assigns the integration lead responsibility for connecting the three items of actual impact, scope, and the old entry. This record still does not invent specific results on behalf of the coordination record. Its value is to let subsequent participants know which three objects to use to reconstruct the decision made at the time, rather than writing results that have not yet occurred into the history.

This review did not change the judgment that "repository evidence takes priority." The change was to apply it to two choices: whether the window should expand must be determined from boundary materials, and whether the old entry can be reverted must be determined from the coordination record. Source locations and call names can still help with identification, but they have not been elevated into proof beyond their own scope.

## Opinions still retained

- The existing materials do not provide a generally applicable way to define the edge of the adjustment window; subsequent discussion should add materials around specific runtime boundaries rather than reuse the wording "the window has already been approved."
- The old entry's long-term retention or removal has not been decided. This round decided only that it must remain as a revertible entry; it did not decide when it may be removed.
- Subsequent organization of the actual impact should be completed in the coordination record; this page does not prematurely state an unrealized replacement or expanded scope as an accomplished fact.
- If the handoff of the Unity package mirror affects adjacent materials, see DOC-52; that handoff record does not change the scope judgment here concerning nightly verifier.

That is the end of the actionable portion of this decision: retain the current entry, limit this round's window, complete the coordination record, and keep unverified items on the review table.

# Unity Mirror Switch Handoff Process

Switching the Unity package mirror was once shortened to "switch to the candidate path." In an actual handoff, consumers are the first to encounter the package entry point change. If the old entry point, the consumer, and the rollback action are not recorded together, anyone coming later sees only a path that has already changed and cannot judge whether the switch should continue.

This record covers known agent-streaming consumers trying the candidate mirror in place of the old entry point. The consumer, not the mirror, is the unit of handoff. Each consumer has its own lifecycle state; until a consumer starts using a candidate path, that path does not constitute a migration result that can be handed off.

```text
Before the switch
Known consumers ──> Old entry point ──> Existing package mirror

Trial in progress
One consumer able to roll back ──> Candidate path ──> Candidate mirror
          │
          └──Return to the old entry point on rollback
```

## Put the Old Entry Point on Record First

Start the inventory with known agent-streaming consumers, not mirror names. For each population included, the handoff record needs to answer four questions: which module it connects to; what lifecycle state it is in; which specific record lets the next owner look back at the path used at the time; and who will provide clarification if anything is ambiguous. That record location can be an existing call record or test record, but it cannot just say "verified."

The handoff constraint is: Every handoff names the module, lifecycle state, concrete evidence path, and the next owner who can disambiguate it. This is not a formatting requirement. Without a module name, the old entry point may be obscured by another package's description; without a lifecycle state, the stage at which rollback occurred cannot be explained; without a record to look back at, the candidate path is only a verbal status; and without someone to take ownership of ambiguities, the inventory cannot serve as a basis for continuing the switch.

The first draft presented "known consumers" as if they were a list ready to migrate. After review, this was corrected: the list defines only the trial scope. The old entry point still needs to be confirmed for each item on the list. They cannot be grouped into the same switch batch just because they all use agent-streaming. This change keeps the first draft's approach to the inventory without treating the inventory as a completion signal.

## Trial Boundaries

Give the candidate path to only one consumer that can roll back independently. Independent rollback means that the consumer can restore the old entry point and record the observations and state at the time that informed the restoration. It does not require waiting for a coordinated replacement on the mirror side, and other known consumers should not have to share the risk of the first trial.

Before the trial, the consumer must document the old entry point and specify the exact location of the record to refer back to. Only then should it start using the candidate path. Stop extending the path to the next batch if an unexplained lifecycle change is observed, the consumer cannot confirm that it can still return to the old entry point, or the caller population is missing from the record. At that point, do not delete the candidate path. Restore that consumer's old entry point and retain the fact that the candidate path was tried.

The rollback record must connect at least three things: which consumer went back; what state it was in before going back; and why it was not possible to continue making a judgment at that point. A record that says only "candidate mirror unavailable" is not useful, because the problem could also be an unconfirmed old entry point, a caller population that has not yet been matched up, or a lifecycle state that was not clearly handed off. After restoring the old entry point, the original candidate path can remain available for the next review, but it must not continue to be shared as a migrated entry point.

## Review Addendum

This review filled gaps in the handoff chain; it did not establish that the mirror switch was complete. At the time of review, the caller populations and rollback actions for some consumers still could not be aligned in a single record, so the page remains marked as migration in progress. Follow-up records should be added under the corresponding consumer, not in a separate progress table that lists only mirror names.

The lookup related to the actual entry point for the Unreal CI window is recorded separately in DOC-53. It can help locate adjacent work, but it does not replace the handoff records here for the Unity package mirror, old entry points, and rollback actions.

Do not expand use of the candidate path until every known consumer has an old entry point, a lifecycle state, a specific record location, and a next owner who can clarify ambiguities. Consumers that have completed the trial must also retain their instructions for restoring the old entry point.

## Trigger

Start this procedure when an on-site message about nightly verifier arrives. Preserve the evidence first; do not write up a cause yet.

## Preserve the evidence

1. Record the mcp-transport version associated with the message; if it cannot be found, write "version missing".
2. Save the unprocessed results; do not rewrite failure output.
3. Save the wrapper diff from the same incident.
4. Put the version, results, and diff in the same record; annotations may be added, but must not replace the originals.

## Choose a branch

If the version and results do not match, stop at version verification; if the results are missing, go back to the message source for the originals; if the diff cannot explain the results, do not write "unrelated"—record only that the relationship is unclear. If all three are present but multiple explanations remain, hand off only the earliest point where you can no longer make a determination.

Every handoff must name the module, lifecycle state, concrete evidence path, and the next person who can resolve the ambiguity in that branch: Every handoff names the module, lifecycle state, concrete evidence path, and the next owner who can disambiguate it.
